# Introduction

Flight delays are among the most costly and disruptive failures in the U.S.
National Airspace System (NAS), and they rarely occur in isolation. A single
late arrival propagates downstream through the same aircraft's rotation and
through shared airport departure and arrival queues, so a local disturbance
becomes a network-wide disruption. Existing airline and airport tools remain
largely retrospective or single-source, reporting delays after they occur rather
than anticipating them from the live state of the airspace.

**Scope.** AeroFlux Stage 2 builds a *scalable, modular, configurable, portable,
and decoupled* big-data platform that ingests, fuses, processes, and analyzes
aviation and weather data in real time. The primary use case is flight-delay
prediction; the same architecture is designed to support congestion analysis,
delay-propagation modeling, operational monitoring, decision support, and
agentic AI. Stage 1 (complete) established a historical machine-learning
pipeline and an interactive prototype; Stage 2 adds the live data platform, a
baseline-versus-advanced model comparison, and an explainable analyst agent.

**Technical challenges.** Building this platform requires solving several
non-trivial problems: (1) ingesting heterogeneous, error-prone streaming sources
(FAA SWIM XML, ADS-B, weather) without data loss; (2) *entity resolution* across
systems that share no universal key—for example, the aircraft tail number is not
published in SWIM flight data and must be recovered from ADS-B; (3) unstable
identifiers, since a flight's `flight_ref` changes on plan amendment while its
Globally Unique Flight Identifier (GUFI) remains stable; (4) train-serve skew,
because historical labels (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) and live
features are measured differently; and (5) delivering all of this at demo quality
on a portable, low-cost footprint.

# Related Work

**Machine-learning delay prediction.** Most prior work frames delay prediction
as supervised classification or regression over historical records. Reviews by
Sternberg et al. (2017) and, more recently, the dissecting review in *IEEE
Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems* (2025) show tree ensembles
and deep networks dominating, with recent studies emphasizing class-imbalance
handling (AlBassam & AlShahrani, 2025). Their strength is high accuracy on curated
historical data; their limitations are that they are retrospective, typically
single-source, and treat flights as independent observations, ignoring the
network coupling that drives real disruptions.

**Delay-propagation modeling.** A separate literature models how delays ripple
through schedules: Beatty et al. (1999) introduced propagation trees, Wong and
Tsai (2012) applied survival models, and Kafle and Zou (2016) proposed an
analytical-econometric approach. These capture the ripple mechanism but are
generally offline and disconnected from real-time streaming prediction.
Belcastro et al. (2016) demonstrated scalable data mining for delay prediction,
establishing the value of big-data tooling but not real-time fusion.

**Operational data fusion.** The state of the art in operational systems is
NASA's Airspace Technology Demonstration 2 (ATD-2) *Fuser* (NASA, 2021), which
fuses multiple SWIM sources into a single GUFI-keyed flight record. Its strength
is production-grade fused "truth"; its limitation is a heavyweight, largely
closed Java stack that is not an open, extensible ML/AI platform.

**Relevance of this approach.** AeroFlux Stage 2 bridges these strands. It
couples lightweight, Fuser-inspired real-time fusion and entity resolution with
propagation-aware feature engineering *and* an explainable retrieval-augmented
agent—integrating capabilities that the prior literature treats separately.

# Objectives

1. Ingest and fuse FAA SWIM, ADS-B, and weather data into a validated, per-flight
   canonical state in real time.
2. Deliver a portable, decoupled platform that runs unchanged on a laptop,
   school hardware, or any cloud VM (container-first, cloud-agnostic).
3. Compare a baseline model against an advanced, propagation- and
   weather-aware model for arrival-delay prediction.
4. Evaluate both **predictive** performance and **system** performance.
5. Provide a starter *Aviation Operations Analyst Agent* that retrieves evidence,
   explains model predictions, and recommends analytical next steps—without
   making operational decisions.
6. Achieve a demonstrable minimum implementation within approximately one month.

# Datasets

The platform fuses four aviation/weather sources plus a documentation corpus,
summarized in @tbl-datasets. FAA SWIM provides the authoritative live NAS flight
state; ADS-B supplies the physical airframe identity (ICAO 24-bit address and
registration) needed to link an aircraft's successive legs; NOAA METAR/TAF
supplies weather, a leading delay driver; and the BTS On-Time Performance
dataset—which includes actual gate times and tail numbers—provides historical
training labels.

| Source | Type | Role | Retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| FAA SWIM (TFMS) | Streaming XML | Live flight state (primary) | 48 h |
| ADS-B (airplanes.live / adsb.lol) | Streaming JSON | Airframe / tail resolution | 48 h |
| NOAA METAR / TAF | Polled | Weather features | 48 h |
| BTS On-Time Performance | Historical CSV | Training labels | Persistent |
| Aviation docs (FAA, SWIM dict.) | Documents | RAG corpus | Persistent |

: Data sources fused by AeroFlux Stage 2. {#tbl-datasets}

# Methodology and Proposed Solution

**Pipeline.** Ingestion services publish each source to a dedicated Kafka topic
(48-hour retention). Apache Spark Structured Streaming consumes these topics and
applies the existing `aeroflux_parser` library to parse, normalize, validate
against a strict schema contract, and fuse messages into per-flight records via
GUFI-keyed, source-priority mediation, with `flight_ref` used only as a
reconciliation bridge and ADS-B used to resolve the tail. Fused records land in
MongoDB (silver, 48-hour TTL) and, together with BTS backfill, in a MinIO
data lake (gold parquet). The full architecture is shown in @fig-arch.

```{mermaid}

  end

    P[Parse + Validate + Fuse]; F[Feature Engineering]
  end
  subgraph ST[Storage]
    M[(MongoDB - 48h TTL)]; L[(MinIO gold parquet)]; PG[(Postgres + pgvector)]
  end
  subgraph MLc[ML]
    B[Baseline: Logistic Reg.]; A[Advanced: XGBoost + propagation]; R[MLflow + SHAP]
  end
  API[FastAPI Inference API]; AG[Analyst Agent - RAG]; UI[AeroFlux UI]

  ADSB --> K
  WX --> K

  F --> L

  L --> A
```

**Baseline versus advanced models.** The baseline is a logistic-regression
classifier on flight-level features (carrier, origin, destination, scheduled
times). The advanced model is a gradient-boosted tree (XGBoost) enriched with
*propagation* features (previous-leg arrival delay, scheduled turnaround buffer),
weather features, and rolling airport demand—directly operationalizing the
propagation literature (Beatty et al., 1999; Kafle & Zou, 2016). Both target a
15-minute arrival-delay classification, with class imbalance addressed via
resampling, a gap noted in recent reviews (AlBassam & AlShahrani, 2025). Models
are tracked in MLflow and explained with SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017), whose
outputs feed the agent.

**Evaluation.** Both predictive and system performance are evaluated
(@tbl-models). Predictive: ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1, and Brier score / calibration,
using point-in-time features to prevent leakage. System: end-to-end latency,
sustained message throughput, fusion completeness (fields populated per flight),
and resource footprint.

| Dimension | Baseline | Advanced | Metrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model | Logistic Regression | XGBoost + propagation + weather | ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1, Brier |
| Features | Flight-level | + propagation, weather, demand | Feature importance (SHAP) |
| System | — | Streaming pipeline | Latency, throughput, completeness |

: Baseline-versus-advanced comparison and evaluation plan. {#tbl-models}

**Agentic AI and LLM approach.** The starter *Aviation Operations Analyst Agent*
answers natural-language questions (e.g., "Why is this flight likely delayed?")
by combining retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) over the
aviation-documentation corpus (embeddings in pgvector) with tool calls that query
the fused databases, invoke the delay model, and return SHAP explanations. The
agent retrieves evidence, explains predictions, and recommends next steps; it
does **not** execute operational aviation decisions.

# Development Environment

The stack (@tbl-stack) is entirely open-source and container-first. Every
component runs as a Docker Compose service, so the platform deploys unchanged on
a laptop, university hardware, or a single cloud VM; managed AWS services (MSK,
EMR, SageMaker) are an optional scale path rather than a requirement. MinIO
provides an S3-compatible object store that swaps to real S3 with no code change.
Short retention keeps storage and cost minimal (target budget: a modest VM plus a
few dollars of LLM API usage).

| Category | Tools |
|---|---|
| Language | Python 3.11 |
| Streaming | Apache Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming |
| Storage | MongoDB, PostgreSQL + pgvector, MinIO (S3-compatible) |
| ML | scikit-learn, XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016), MLflow, SHAP |
| LLM / RAG | Claude API, pgvector, tool-calling agent loop |
| Serving / UI | FastAPI, Dash / Plotly |
| Orchestration | Prefect |
| Packaging / Platform | Docker + Docker Compose; optional AWS EC2 + S3 |

: Development environment and technology stack. {#tbl-stack}

# Project Tasks and Timeline

The minimum implementation is scoped to approximately one month (@tbl-timeline),
building on Stage 1's completed ingestion, fusion, entity-resolution, schema
contract, and baseline model. Future capabilities—graph analytics, simulation,
digital twin, and a multi-agent system—are explicitly out of scope for this
timeline.

| Week | Tasks | Est. hours |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add weather source; Spark Structured Streaming pipeline; MongoDB silver store + TTL | 20 |
| 2 | Feature engineering (propagation, demand, weather); gold dataset; baseline vs. advanced training; MLflow; evaluation | 22 |
| 3 | FastAPI inference API + SHAP; pgvector RAG; analyst agent + tools | 22 |
| 4 | Integration, UI wiring, system + predictive evaluation, demo, write-up; buffer | 18 |

: One-month project timeline and effort allocation. {#tbl-timeline}
